titleEn: God of my praise, do not be silent
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Thirty-one verses of a man attacked by speech, answering with speech. The middle block, verses 6 to 19, is a curse violent enough that translators disagree about whose mouth it belongs in: the JPS version this page is built from puts the whole block inside quotation marks and reads it as the enemies' words quoted back at them. The psalm has no fixed place in the daily service, so most readers meet it only going through the book in order. Watch one detail travel the whole length: the accuser told to stand at the right hand in verse 6 is answered exactly in verse 31, where God stands at the right hand of the poor man.

stichs.en: For the leader. A psalm of David.
God of my praise, do not stay silent.

verses.summary: The first request of the psalm is not for rescue but for speech. The whole book is called Tehilim, praises, and the speaker addresses God by that word before saying anything else.

stichs.en: For a wicked mouth and a mouth of deceit have opened against me;
they have spoken to me with a tongue of lies.

verses.summary: The reason for the request. Two mouths open where one silence was asked to end, and the attack has no weapon in it except language.

stichs.en: And with words of hatred they surrounded me,
and fought me for nothing.

verses.summary: Words become terrain: they encircle. The last word insists there was no cause, which is what makes this a legal complaint rather than a lament.

stichs.en: In return for my love they accuse me,
and I am prayer.

verses.summary: The shortest and strangest clause in the psalm. The Hebrew does not say I pray; it puts the noun where a verb should be, so the speaker is the thing itself.

stichs.en: They laid evil on me in return for good,
and hatred in return for my love.

verses.summary: The exchange is stated twice with the same preposition, once for deeds and once for feeling. The repetition closes the complaint and opens what follows.

stichs.en: Appoint a wicked man over him,
and let an accuser stand at his right hand.

verses.summary: The curse begins, and the plural enemies of verses 2 to 5 collapse into a single him. Whether the speaker says this or reports it is the central question of the psalm.

stichs.en: When he is judged, let him come out guilty,
and let his prayer count as a sin.

verses.summary: The scene is a courtroom, and the verdict is asked for in advance. The second half is the harshest line so far, because it takes away the one move left to a condemned man.

stichs.en: Let his days be few;
let someone else take his office.

verses.summary: The noun in the second half means an appointed charge, a post someone holds. The curse is not only that he dies but that he is replaced and the work continues without him.

stichs.en: Let his sons be orphans,
and his wife a widow.

verses.summary: The curse moves from the man to the people who depend on him, which is exactly the class the Torah protects most explicitly. That collision is deliberate and uncomfortable.

stichs.en: Let his sons wander and wander, and beg,
let them scavenge out of their ruins.

verses.summary: The doubled verb, the infinitive next to the finite form, is the standard Hebrew way of intensifying: not just wander but wander and keep wandering.

stichs.en: Let a creditor seize everything he has,
and let strangers plunder what he earned.

verses.summary: The estate goes next. The last word means labour in the sense of what labour produced, so what is taken is the man's work rather than his property.

stichs.en: Let there be no one to extend kindness to him,
and no one to show favour to his orphans.

verses.summary: The word for kindness here is chesed, the covenant word, and the curse is that no one draws it out toward him. It is a curse aimed at bystanders as much as at the man.

stichs.en: Let what comes after him be cut off;
in the next generation let their name be wiped out.

verses.summary: Erasure of the name is the deepest curse available in this literature, because a name carried by descendants is the only continuity the Hebrew Bible reliably promises.

stichs.en: Let the guilt of his fathers be remembered before the LORD,
and let his mother's sin not be wiped away.

verses.summary: The same verb that wiped out the name in verse 13 is now refused to the parents' sin. What the man loses, his record keeps.

stichs.en: Let them be before the LORD continually,
and let Him cut their memory off from the earth.

verses.summary: Two opposite kinds of remembering in one verse: permanently present to God, entirely absent from the world. The curse is precise about which memory it wants destroyed.

stichs.en: Because he did not remember to do kindness,
and hunted down a poor and needy man,
and the broken in heart, to kill him.

verses.summary: The only verse in the curse block that gives a reason, and it is the exact charge the speaker will turn back on himself in verse 22: he too is poor and needy.

stichs.en: He loved cursing, and it came to him;
he took no delight in blessing, and it stayed far from him.

verses.summary: The logic shifts from punishment to consequence. Cursing and blessing behave like things with their own motion, arriving or withdrawing according to what a man wanted.

stichs.en: He wore cursing as his clothing,
and it came into his insides like water,
and into his bones like oil.

verses.summary: Three degrees of absorption in one verse: worn, drunk, soaked into the bone. Speech is treated as a substance that penetrates the body of the one who spoke it.

stichs.en: Let it be for him like the coat he wraps around himself,
and like the belt he ties on every day.

verses.summary: The clothing image from verse 18 returns and closes the block. In the JPS translation this is where the quotation mark shuts.

stichs.en: This is the wage of my accusers from the LORD,
of those who speak evil against my life.

verses.summary: One verse seals the block and hands it back to God. The word for wage means what work earns, so the curse is presented as payment rather than as spite.

stichs.en: But You, LORD my Lord, act with me for Your name's sake;
because Your kindness is good, rescue me.

verses.summary: The hinge. The address turns from the enemy to God, and the reason given is not the speaker's innocence but God's name and God's kindness.

stichs.en: For I am poor and needy,
and my heart is pierced inside me.

verses.summary: The speaker takes for himself the exact two words used in verse 16 for the victim the enemy hunted. The accusation and the self-description now match.

stichs.en: Like a shadow as it stretches out, I am going;
I am shaken off like a locust.

verses.summary: A shadow at the end of the day is longest just before it disappears. Both images are passive: the speaker is not leaving, he is being removed.

stichs.en: My knees give way from fasting,
and my flesh has grown lean, with no fat on it.

verses.summary: The complaint becomes physical and specific. Fasting here is what the speaker did to himself while praying, so the body is evidence of the prayer.

stichs.en: And I have become a mockery to them;
they look at me and shake their heads.

verses.summary: Back to speech, or rather to the gesture that replaces it. The head shake is a public verdict delivered without a word.

stichs.en: Help me, LORD my God;
save me in keeping with Your kindness.

verses.summary: Two imperatives with the object suffix attached, the shortest verse of the plea. The measure asked for is chesed again, the same word the enemy failed to show in verse 16.

stichs.en: Let them know that this is Your hand,
that You, LORD, have done it.

verses.summary: The point of the rescue is not comfort but demonstration. The speaker wants the same audience that mocked him to read the outcome correctly.

stichs.en: Let them curse, but You will bless;
they rose up and were shamed, but Your servant is glad.

verses.summary: Cursing and blessing are set side by side one last time, and the speaker concedes the enemy the right to keep cursing. He is no longer asking for their mouths to be shut.

stichs.en: Let my accusers be dressed in humiliation,
and wrapped in their own shame like a robe.

verses.summary: The clothing image from verses 18 and 19 comes back, now in the speaker's own undisputed voice and aimed at the plural accusers rather than one man.

stichs.en: I will thank the LORD greatly with my mouth,
and among many I will praise Him.

verses.summary: The speaker's mouth finally appears, thirty verses after the enemies' mouths opened. The answer to public slander is public praise, in front of the same crowd.

stichs.en: Because He stands at the right hand of the needy,
to save him from those who sentence his life.

verses.summary: The last verse answers verse 6 word for word. The position an accuser was asked to take at the wicked man's right hand is the position God takes beside the poor man.

pardes.body: Five parts. Verses 1 to 5 are the complaint, and every weapon in them is verbal. Verses 6 to 19 are a sustained curse against a single man, his office, his family, his estate and his name. Verse 20 seals that block and hands it to God as a wage owed. Verses 21 to 25 turn to God and describe a body wrecked by fasting and public contempt. Verses 26 to 31 ask for rescue, promise public thanks, and close on the image the curse opened with. The clearest structural fact in the psalm is the pair of right hands: an accuser is told to stand at the right hand of the accused in verse 6, and in verse 31 God stands at the right hand of the needy. Same posture, opposite courtroom.

One root runs the length of the psalm: the root behind {{6.3}}, the word satan, which here is a common noun for a courtroom accuser and not a proper name. It appears as a verb in {{4.2}}, they accuse me, and as a plural noun in {{20.2}} and again in {{29.1}}. Reading those four points in order gives the plot without the sentences. The other crux is who speaks verses 6 to 19. The Hebrew has no quotation marks, and the block can be read either as the speaker's own curse or as the enemies' curse quoted back so that verse 20 can call it their wage. The JPS translation printed in this project's source file takes the second option and opens a quotation mark at verse 6, closing it at the end of verse 19. Both readings are old, and neither is settled. Note also {{4.4}}: the Hebrew is a noun, prayer, not a verb, so the line says the speaker is prayer rather than that he prays.

One line of traditional reading refuses to leave the target anonymous and attaches the psalm to named enemies out of the David narratives, which turns an open curse into a verdict on a person the reader already knows and limits how far it can be reused. A second line works on {{4.4}} and reads it as a description of a state rather than an activity: a man so far into his situation that prayer is no longer something he does at intervals but what he now consists of. A third, less comfortable, notices that verses 9 and 12 curse orphans and widows, the two groups the Torah names most often as protected, and treats the psalm as showing what rage produces when it is given full speech instead of being acted on. On that reading the block is preserved precisely because it was said and not done.

The psalm is built out of mouths. It opens with the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit in {{2.1}} and {{2.3}}, and it does not reach the speaker's own mouth until {{30.3}}, twenty-eight verses later. In between, cursing stops being sound and becomes matter: worn as clothing, drunk like water in {{18.4}}, soaked into the bones like oil. That is the mystical reading in condensed form, that speech is a substance and takes on the shape of whoever holds it, so a man who loves cursing ends up wearing it. The turn at verse 21 is therefore not a change of subject but a change of what the speaker's own speech is being used for, and the last word of the psalm is a mouth speaking praise in front of a crowd rather than a mouth speaking harm behind a back.
